sections.h2: Where is Lawrence, Kansas, and what does the city look like?
sections.html:
Lawrence is a Douglas County city about 25 miles east of Topeka and 35 miles west of Kansas City, Kansas. It sits between the Kansas River and the Wakarusa River, which shapes both its streets and its flood maps.

The Census Bureau puts the city at 34.26 square miles, with the highest ground on Mount Oread, where the University of Kansas campus stands at 1,020 feet. Several creeks cross town. Burroughs Creek runs through East Lawrence, Baldwin Creek drains the northwest, and Yankee Tank Creek in the southwest feeds Lake Alvamar before reaching the Wakarusa.

Lawrence also has 54 parks and a planned 22-mile Lawrence Loop trail that circles the city. For a seller, that mix of campus, river valley and park land means two houses a mile apart can sit in very different settings, and buyers notice it.

sections.h2: What is the history behind Lawrence houses?
sections.html:
Lawrence was founded in 1854 by antislavery settlers, so some of its housing stock is among the oldest in Kansas. On August 21, 1863, William Quantrill's raiders destroyed most of the town's houses and businesses, so the oldest surviving buildings mostly come from the rebuilding that followed.

Older neighborhoods close to downtown, such as Old West Lawrence, North Lawrence, East Lawrence, Oread, Hancock and Pinkney, tend to hold older homes. Farther west, past Iowa Street, are Sunset Hills, Prairie Meadows, Deerfield and Alvamar. Age matters when you sell. An older house may carry original wiring, plumbing or a stone foundation, and a conventional buyer's lender and inspector will ask about each of them.

sections.h2: What drives the Lawrence economy and housing demand?
sections.html:
Education is the center of the local economy. The University of Kansas was the largest employer in the city as of 2020, with 10,116 employees, followed by Maximus, Lawrence Memorial Hospital and Hallmark Cards.

A university town has a housing rhythm of its own. Leases tend to turn over in summer, and the city's own rental inspection rules reflect that: Lawrence does not schedule required rental inspections in July or August unless the owner asks. If you own a rental near campus, the calendar can affect when a vacant house is easiest to show or hand over.

The city also had a rise in homelessness after 2019, and in February 2023 the City Commission passed an ordinance banning source of income discrimination, so landlords cannot turn away housing vouchers. Landlords thinking of selling a tenant-occupied house should know that rule exists.

sections.h2: Which roads and transit connect Lawrence to the rest of the region?
sections.html:
Interstate 70, which runs here as the Kansas Turnpike, crosses the northern edge of the city. U.S. 59 runs north and south along Iowa Street, and U.S. 40 follows 6th Street. K-10 reaches Kansas City by way of the South Lawrence Trafficway, which was connected in November 2016, and the Kansas Department of Transportation began widening the western stretch to four lanes in 2024.

Two bus systems serve the city: Lawrence Transit, known as The T, and KU on Wheels. Together they run 18 routes. Kansas City International Airport is roughly 50 miles northeast of downtown. The commute to the Kansas City area is one reason some owners keep a Lawrence house for years, and one reason a buyer may accept a longer drive for a lower price.

sections.h2: What is the climate in Lawrence, and what does it do to a house?
sections.html:
Lawrence has a humid continental climate with hot, humid summers and cold, dry winters. The table below uses 1991 to 2020 normals from the long Lawrence record.

MeasureLawrence normal
Average July daily high88.6 F
Average January daily low19.4 F
Annual precipitation39.40 inches
Annual snowfall10.4 inches
Record high114 F, August 1934
Wettest monthsMay (5.13 in) and June (5.69 in)

Spring is the wet season, with May near 5.13 inches and June near 5.69. Heavy spring rain is hard on basements, gutters and older roofs. Wide swings between a freezing winter and a hot summer also stress siding, driveways and foundations. Those are the items a buyer's inspector writes up first, so they are also the items that drag a conventional sale into repair negotiations.

sections.h2: Do Lawrence rental licensing rules affect a sale?
sections.html:
Yes, if the house is rented. Lawrence requires a license for every rental dwelling unit in the city, renewed each year, under Ordinance 8840, adopted April 1, 2014.

The city's FAQ lists several points that matter to an owner who wants out:

  • Vacant rental units must still be licensed.
  • A house under contract to be bought by its tenant stays on the licensing rolls until the buyer's name is recorded with the Douglas County Register of Deeds.
  • If the owner lives elsewhere and a relative lives in the house, it is exempt. If that relative has an unrelated roommate, it must be licensed.
  • Required inspections run on a 3-year or 6-year cycle depending on how many violations were found, and the owner or agent must attend.
  • A notice of violation generally gives 30 days to fix items, and an appeal goes to the Building Code Board of Appeals within 14 days.

Failing to license a rental before renting it may be prosecuted in municipal court. Occupancy limits also matter: the city's zoning rules allow up to three unrelated occupants in single-family districts and four in most other districts. An investor or an heir who inherits a rental with an expired license or open violations can find that a normal listing stalls. A buyer who takes the house as-is does not need the license fixed before closing.

sections.h2: What should a Lawrence seller know about taxes and the county offices?
sections.html:
Property tax in Lawrence is billed by Douglas County. The county treasurer's office is at 2601 West 6th Street, and the Register of Deeds is in the county courthouse at 1100 Massachusetts Street.

The Douglas County Treasurer explains the residential formula this way: appraised value times 11.5 percent gives assessed value, and assessed value times the mill levy, divided by 1,000, gives the estimated tax. The first half of the tax bill is due on or before December 20, and the treasurer takes calls at 785-832-5178 for tax questions.

ItemDouglas County detail
Residential assessment rate11.5% of appraised value
Payment window noted by treasurerAfter November 1 and on or before December 20
Treasurer office2601 W. 6th Street, Lawrence
Register of Deeds1100 Massachusetts Street, 785-832-5282
Card payment fee at treasurer2.35%, 50 cent minimum

At closing, the title company normally prorates the year's tax between buyer and seller, so ask for a payoff and proration figure early. If taxes are behind, the treasurer's page on tax foreclosures shows how the county handles them.

sections.h2: How does recording a deed work in Douglas County?
sections.html:
The Douglas County Register of Deeds records deeds, mortgages, plats and other real estate documents, and a title company or attorney generally handles the filing for a sale.

The office accepts electronic recordings from four named vendors: Simplifile, Mobilis, CSC and ePN. Documents for property in the county must carry the full legal description, and the office advises against abbreviated descriptions. The county publishes a Kansas Real Estate Sales Validation Questionnaire, which is part of how a sale price is reported.

The office does not prepare deeds and recommends that a title company or attorney do it, since a drafting error can change ownership in ways that are costly to fix. It also runs a free Real Estate Fraud Alert service: you enroll by name and get an email when a matching name is indexed. An owner who inherited a Lawrence house, or who lives out of town, may find that useful while the property sits vacant.

sections.h2: What are the main ways to sell a house in Lawrence?
sections.html:
There are three practical routes: list with an agent, sell it yourself, or accept a cash offer from a buyer who purchases as-is.

  • Listing: best when the house is in good shape and you can wait through showings, inspection requests and a buyer's loan approval.
  • Selling yourself: saves an agent's fee but puts marketing, disclosures and paperwork on you.
  • Cash offer: suits a vacant rental, an inherited house, a property with code violations or a seller who needs a firm closing date.

In Lawrence, cash tends to come up with student rentals that need work after a hard lease year, with inherited houses in older neighborhoods, and with owners who live elsewhere. Whatever the route, compare the net figure after repairs, carrying costs and time, not only the headline number. We buy houses in Lawrence as-is, and you can request an offer without obligation.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental license to sell a rented house in Lawrence?
faqs.a: You need the license to keep renting, but not to sell. Lawrence requires a license for each rental unit, including vacant ones, until a buyer's name is recorded as owner with the Douglas County Register of Deeds. Letting a license lapse while tenants remain can bring municipal court action.

faqs.q: When are Douglas County property taxes due?
faqs.a: The first half or the full amount is due on or before December 20. The Douglas County Treasurer receives payments after November 1, and tax questions go to 785-832-5178.

faqs.q: Where is a deed recorded for a Lawrence house?
faqs.a: At the Douglas County Register of Deeds, 1100 Massachusetts Street in Lawrence. Title companies usually record electronically through a vendor such as Simplifile, so the seller seldom files the deed personally.

faqs.q: Does the University of Kansas affect when a house sells?
faqs.a: It affects rentals most. The university is the city's largest employer, summer is the busy lease turnover period, and the city does not schedule required rental inspections in July or August unless the owner requests one.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lawrence house with code or inspection problems?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer purchases as-is, so open violations, deferred repairs or a failed rental inspection do not have to be fixed first. A conventional buyer's lender and inspector will usually require those items to be addressed.
